Split it as _The students / are learning_: **S V**.

The following passage contains **subject–verb agreement (concord) errors**. Identify and correct them. Do **not** copy the passage.

> The saving of certain wild animals have, for many years, been a problem for zoologists and other specialists. Currently, scholarly research shows that a number of factors has contributed in making the problem so acute. One of the major contributing factors is the lack of strict laws to protect wild animals. There seem also to be an increase in the hunting of these animals for domestic purposes. This second set of factors send a strong signal that more wild animals faces threat of extinction if the trend of these murders continue. Finally, the march of civilising cultures is a factor. When an area of animals is wholly cleared of vegetation to make room for new towns, factory sites or hydroelectric plants, the natural home of several species are destroyed. It is sad that civilisation, which can bring so many benefits to people, cause a lot of harm to wild animals as it threaten their disappearance from the earth. Animals that protect the environment needs to be saved.
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. _The saving … have_ → **The saving … has** (head: _saving_)
> 2. _a number of factors has contributed_ → **a number of factors have contributed** (_a number of_ = plural)
> 3. _There seem also to be an increase_ → **There seems also to be an increase** (subject: _an increase_)
> 4. _This second set of factors send_ → **This second set of factors sends** (head: _set_)
> 5. _more wild animals faces_ → **more wild animals face**
> 6. _the trend of these murders continue_ → **the trend of these murders continues** (head: _trend_)
> 7. _the natural home of several species are destroyed_ → **the natural home of several species is destroyed** (head: _home_)
> 8. _civilisation, which …, cause_ → **civilisation, which …, causes**
> 9. _it threaten_ → **it threatens**
> 10. _Animals that protect the environment needs_ → **Animals that protect the environment need**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Concord (subject–verb agreement)**: the verb agrees with the **head** of the subject, not with nouns in phrases after it (_The use of drones … **is**_); **relative pronouns** take the number of their antecedent (_students who **seek**_); **as well as / together with / along with** do not make a subject plural; with **neither … nor / either … or** the verb agrees with the nearer subject; **each / every / one of / many a** take singular verbs; **a number of** is plural, **the number of** singular.

## Simplified explanation

Match each verb to its real subject: **saving has, factors have, an increase seems, set sends, animals face, trend continues, home is, civilisation causes, it threatens, animals need**.
hint: Find the head noun of each subject, then check its verb.

The following passage contains **subject–verb agreement (concord) errors**. Identify and correct them. Do **not** copy the passage.

> The Dean, as well as the committee, are gathered in the boardroom today because the series of recent incidents make a formal review necessary. While the faculty is currently debating the new curriculum in the hall, it has been recommended that the chairman postpone the final vote. Neither the professors nor the student representative want to rush this decision, as every student and teacher expect a fair process.
>
> Earlier, it was noted that a pair of scissors lie forgotten on the podium. Many a candidate have complained about the lack of equipment, yet ten percent of the budget go toward administrative costs rather than new supplies. Our Head of Department and lead researcher are currently preparing a report, while the police works to ensure campus security remain tight.
>
> Finally, one of the farmers who works the university lands have requested a meeting. Each of the members are required to attend, for as we know, all are lost if we fail to communicate.
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. _The Dean, as well as the committee, are_ → **The Dean, as well as the committee, is** (_as well as_ does not add)
> 2. _the series of recent incidents make_ → **the series of recent incidents makes** (_series_ = one sequence)
> 3. _Neither the professors nor the student representative want_ → **… the student representative wants** (nearer subject singular)
> 4. _every student and teacher expect_ → **every student and teacher expects** (_every_ = singular)
> 5. _a pair of scissors lie_ → **a pair of scissors lies (or _lay_, after _was noted_)** (head: _pair_)
> 6. _Many a candidate have complained_ → **Many a candidate has complained** (_many a_ = singular)
> 7. _ten percent of the budget go_ → **ten percent of the budget goes** (percentage of a singular noun)
> 8. _Our Head of Department and lead researcher are_ → **Our Head of Department and lead researcher is** (one person with two titles)
> 9. _the police works_ → **the police work** (_police_ is plural)
> 10. _campus security remain_ → **campus security remains**
> 11. _one of the farmers who works_ → **one of the farmers who work** (_who_ = farmers)
> 12. _one of the farmers … have requested_ → **one of the farmers … has requested** (head: _one_)
> 13. _Each of the members are_ → **Each of the members is**
> 14. _all are lost_ → **all is lost** (_all_ = everything)
>
> __postpone_ after _recommended that_ is a correct subjunctive; _the faculty is_ is also correct._

> [!answer]
> Yesterday, when I heard that Zawusi Woods Limited had spent a small fortune clearing only three **pieces** of equipment for the company's sawmill, **I** went to see my brother, Joe Ewusi, the managing director. I asked Joe, “**Why** are three small units of machinery very expensive?” Joe then gave me a lesson on wood technology. **QUESTION 1.** Read the following passage carefully, and either write an **OUTLINE** or **SUMMARISE** it in between **100 and 120 words**.

> Depression is a common mental disorder that affects anyone anywhere. Most women have major depression during their lifetime. Once they pass menopause, women become less prone to depression. 13 out of every 100 men, during their lifetime, cope with some forms of depression. Children up to the age of 10 may experience depression, though the gender differences are not apparent until the reproductive years.
>
> The symptoms of depression vary from person to person. Persistent tiredness and loss of energy are common complaints among those suffering from it. Depressed individuals may suffer from loss of concentration and become indecisive. Feelings of guilt and low self-worth often persist for weeks and even months at a time. Some may experience difficulty in sleeping or, on the other hand, sleep more than normal. Many find themselves waking up early. Persons suffering from depression tend to lose interest in daily activities. They may struggle with re-occurring thoughts of death and suicide. In severe cases, individuals with depression lose interest in eating and no longer find pleasure in any of life's activities.
>
> The cause of depression is not the same for everybody. For some, it is a genetic problem that affects the balance of chemicals in the brain. For others, a stressful life event, such as the death of a loved one, losing a job or a divorce may trigger it. In many cases, depression occurs as a result of the combination of both the chemical imbalance and a triggering event. Another factor that may influence the onset of depression is the hormonal fluctuations of the reproductive years. The demands placed on women to produce or regulate family size mean that they often carry disproportionate responsibilities and accountability for reproductive function. Infertility or miscarriage may get viewed as a failure to fulfil this role. Oral contraceptives may carry a potential for depression in susceptible women. Whatever the cause, whether it is a chemical upset in the brain or the heartache of some major life events, depression can harm a person's life and needs effective solutions.
>
> There exists a number of approaches to the treatment of major depression. A person with a major depressive illness will need professional help. Careful evaluation will help to determine the precise form of treatment needed. Severe cases may call for hospital admission. …
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Model summary (100–120 words):**
>
> **Depression: its prevalence, symptoms, causes and treatment**
>
> Depression is a common mental disorder that can affect anyone. Women are especially prone until menopause, many men also suffer, and even young children may experience it. Its symptoms differ from person to person but include constant tiredness, poor concentration, indecision, lasting guilt and low self-esteem, disturbed sleep, loss of interest in daily life and food, and recurring thoughts of death. Its causes also vary: some people inherit a chemical imbalance in the brain, others react to stressful events such as bereavement, job loss or divorce, and many face both. In women, hormonal changes and reproductive pressures, including infertility, miscarriage and some contraceptives, add to the risk. Because depression can ruin lives, sufferers need careful professional evaluation and treatment, and severe cases may require hospitalisation. (about 115 words)
>
> _Outline alternative:_ (1) Prevalence: anyone; women before menopause; men; children. (2) Symptoms: fatigue, poor concentration, guilt, sleep problems, loss of interest, suicidal thoughts. (3) Causes: genetic chemical imbalance; stressful events; hormonal/reproductive factors in women. (4) Treatment: professional evaluation; hospital care for severe cases.

**SECTION A (30 marks).** Read the following passage carefully, and either write an **outline** or **summarise** it in between **100 and 120 words**.

> The phenomenon of migration is increasingly maintaining its place on the agenda day-by-day. Migration is the movement of people in order to live in a place other than where they are. Identifications regarding the nature and causes of migration are discussed.
>
> First, migration can take place within or outside the borders of the country, singularly or in mass. Thus, migration is defined differently as internal migration within the borders of the country (national) or immigration from abroad to that country or from that country to another country (international). Second, distinctions are created between regular and irregular migration. Regular migration is defined as the short-term or long-term stay of individuals in any country or in different regions of their own country, within the framework of legal permissions. Irregular migration is illegally entering a country, staying in a country illegally or not leaving the country despite entering legally, in the following period despite the expiry of the legal period.
>
> Political reasons constitute a large part of the migration movements occurring on a global scale. Factors such as human rights violations due to political reasons, persecution, restriction of personal freedoms, inequalities, lack of judicial independence, and military coups constitute the main reasons for migration movements. Unfortunately, the most dominant actor of political reasons is wars. Wars that cause great migration movements are also one of the main reasons for forced migration.
>
> A wide range of social factors create migration. Many reasons such as people's desire to be with their families or relatives who have migrated before, and the fact that the target country speaks the same language can force people to migrate. Also, the characteristics that they feel close to them culturally and socially, and the desire to get a better education and freedom of belief can be examined under this heading. High fertility rates and the incidence of infectious diseases can also cause migration. Migration may be a choice for people with a high population living together in relatively small houses and sharing limited space with many siblings and family members.
>
> Natural factors have created reasons for migration throughout history, but a significant increase has been observed in the last 100 years. In particular, this increase has an impact on internal migration. Changing climatic conditions caused by global warming have a great impact on natural factors. We have seen floods, fires, droughts, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landslides, tsunamis and similar disasters of a type and extent that mankind has not encountered before. Migration continues to create human movements of unavoidable magnitude.
>
> International cooperation on migration is of great importance. There is a need for dynamic policies in terms of receiving and sending migrants from and to countries. A good understanding of the reasons that trigger migration is very important in terms of solving the problem at its source. The best solution to a problem is possible by eliminating its causes.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Model summary (100–120 words):**
>
> **Migration: types, causes and solutions**
>
> Migration, the movement of people to live somewhere else, is a growing global concern. It may be internal or international, and regular, when it follows legal permission, or irregular, when people enter or stay in a country illegally. Political factors cause much of it: persecution, human-rights abuses, loss of freedoms, inequality, coups and, above all, wars, which force people to flee. Social factors also contribute, including the wish to join relatives, shared language and culture, better education, religious freedom, high fertility, disease and overcrowded homes. Natural disasters, increasingly worsened by global warming, now drive large movements, especially within countries. Because migration is so extensive, countries must cooperate on flexible policies and tackle its root causes. (about 118 words)
>
> _Outline alternative:_ (1) Definition and importance. (2) Types: internal/international; regular/irregular. (3) Political causes, especially war. (4) Social causes. (5) Natural causes and climate change. (6) Solutions: international cooperation; tackling root causes.

Read the text below and **summarise** it in between **150 and 160 words**.

> A training need exists when there is a gap between what someone can do and what he should be able to do. Training should be designed to fill that gap.
>
> The basic purpose of training is the transfer of skills from those who have them to those who do not. Just having the skills is not enough to be an effective trainer. Anyone responsible for training should understand how best to impart knowledge or skills. … something that will benefit them as well as the company. They must not feel threatened.
>
> Robert Townsend's approach to training in Up the Organization is simple: "The only way I know to get somebody trained is on the job." This statement expresses a fundamental truth. People learn best by doing. Training off the job is too often irrelevant and there is always the problem of transferring what is learnt on a course back to the workplace. Effective transfer of learning is possible if the off-the-job training simulates working conditions with a reasonable degree of precision, but this is often difficult to accomplish.
>
> Training off the job is, however, appropriate in some circumstances. For example, it is often quicker and cheaper to train fitters and machinists in their basic skills in a separate workshop. And some knowledge, for example, of how to operate a new machine, may only be obtainable outside the organization.
>
> But the fact remains that most learning takes place on the job, and its effectiveness depends on whether managers and supervisors are able to carry out training as one of their key responsibilities.
>
> Off-the-job training can be of benefit to managers and supervisors. Action-centred techniques which involve trainees directly in real work problems, while providing them with the help and guidance of external tutors, have proved effective. Managers can also benefit from the broadening effect of an external course which enables them to reflect and build upon their own experience and, more importantly, to meet and talk with other managers. Don't worry if they come back and say they learn more in the bar than in the classroom. It's where they learn that matters, not how they learn it. Nevertheless, on-the-job training is still the best way of developing managers, especially if it is properly organized.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Model summary (150–160 words):**
>
> **On-the-job and off-the-job training**
>
> A training need arises when there is a gap between what people can do and what they should be able to do, and training aims to close it by passing skills from those who have them to those who lack them. Trainers therefore need more than skill: they must know how to teach, and trainees must see the benefit to themselves and the company without feeling threatened. People learn best by doing, so training on the job is generally the most effective. Off-the-job courses often prove irrelevant and are hard to apply at work unless they closely imitate real working conditions. Nevertheless, they are useful in some cases: basic skills for fitters and machinists can be taught more quickly and cheaply in a separate workshop, and some knowledge, such as how to operate a new machine, can only be obtained outside. Since most learning still happens at work, managers and supervisors must accept training as a key duty. Managers themselves gain from action-centred courses on real problems and from external courses that broaden them and let them share ideas with other managers, but properly organised on-the-job training remains the best way to develop them. (about 155 words)
>
> _Outline alternative:_ (1) Training need = skills gap. (2) Purpose: transfer of skills; trainers must know how to teach. (3) On-the-job training is best: learning by doing. (4) Off-the-job training: often irrelevant, but useful for basic skills and specialist knowledge. (5) Managers and supervisors must train. (6) Managers benefit from external and action-centred courses, but on-the-job development is still best.

Study the passage below carefully, and then write an **OUTLINE** of it.

> There are times human beings catch cold. Cold can be caused by more than 200 different viruses. One unique virus that can cause cold is a rhinovirus which affects the nose. In fact, everybody stands the chance of catching a cold. Common cold also known as cold is a viral infectious disease of the upper respiratory tract that primarily affects the nose, the throat, sinuses and the larynx.
>
> Cold viruses are released into the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. The viruses can remain in the air for a while, and people can inhale them and become infected. They also can become infected by shaking hands with an infected person or by touching objects contaminated with the viruses – if they then touch a mucous membrane with the virus-contaminated hand (rub their eye or nose, touch inside their mouth), the viruses can pass into their blood-stream.
>
> Symptoms include runny nose, watery eyes, difficulty in breathing, sneezing, sore throat, coughs and headache and can last from two to fourteen days.
>
> People with colds need to get plenty of rest and drink plenty of fluids. Over-the-counter (OTC) medicines may help relieve some symptoms, but they will not cure or shorten the length of a cold. Gargling with warm salt water can bring relief to a sore throat. Applying petroleum jelly to the nose may help an irritated nose.
>
> The most effective way to keep from getting a cold is to wash the hands frequently and not touch the nose or eyes, sneeze or cough into a facial tissue. Whenever possible, avoid close contact with anyone who has a cold. To keep colds from spreading in a family, wash dishes and other objects thoroughly in hot, soapy water or in a dishwasher.
>
> In conclusion, because there are more than 200 viruses that cause the common cold, colds are so common and often return. The human body can never build up resistance to all the viruses.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Model summary (outline):**
>
> Prose summary (alternative to the outline): The common cold is a viral infection of the upper respiratory tract caused by more than 200 viruses, such as the rhinovirus, so anyone can catch it. It spreads through infected droplets in the air and through touching infected people or objects and then the eyes, nose or mouth. Symptoms such as a runny nose, sneezing, a sore throat, coughing and headache last up to two weeks. Rest, fluids and simple remedies ease the symptoms but do not cure it. Washing hands, avoiding contact with sufferers and cleaning shared items prevent its spread. Because the viruses are so many, the body cannot become immune to all of them.
>
> _Outline alternative:_ **Title: The Common Cold**
> 1. Nature and cause: (a) a viral infection of the upper respiratory tract (nose, throat, sinuses, larynx); (b) over 200 viruses, e.g. rhinovirus; (c) anyone can catch it.
> 2. Mode of transmission: (a) inhaling viruses released by coughs and sneezes; (b) handshakes and contaminated objects, then touching eyes, nose or mouth.
> 3. Symptoms: runny nose, watery eyes, breathing difficulty, sneezing, sore throat, cough, headache; 2–14 days.
> 4. Management: (a) rest and fluids; (b) OTC medicines relieve but do not cure; (c) salt-water gargle; (d) petroleum jelly for the nose.
> 5. Prevention: (a) frequent hand-washing; (b) not touching the face; (c) using tissues; (d) avoiding sufferers; (e) washing dishes in hot, soapy water.
> 6. Conclusion: many viruses, so no lasting immunity.

Read the passage below carefully and **summarise** it in **not more than 150 words**.

> The geographical spread of English is unique among the languages of the world, not only in our time but throughout history. English is the majority first language in twenty-three countries. It is an official language or a joint official language in about fifty other countries, where it is used in addition to the indigenous first languages for a variety of public and personal functions. It is also used as a second language, though with official status, in countries such as Bangladesh and Malaysia. Countries where English is a first or second language are located in all five continents. The total population of these countries amounts to around 2.5 billion, about 49 per cent of the world's population. Where English is a first or second language, it is used internally for communication between nationals of the same country. In addition, English is used extensively as a foreign language for international communication by people who do not ordinarily employ it when speaking or writing to their compatriots.
>
> The number of first language speakers of English has been estimated at well over 300 million, of whom over 216 million live in the United States. The United Kingdom has about 53 million, Canada over 17 million, and Australia about 14 million. Countries where English is a majority first language may have large percentages of bilingual speakers and speakers for whom English is a second language. For example, Canada has a large minority of unilingual French speakers (nearly 17 per cent) as well as an almost equal percentage of speakers who are bilingual in French and English.
>
> Most countries with second-language speakers of English are former British colonies, such as India and Nigeria. English has been retained as an official language in the majority of these countries after independence because none of the indigenous languages was accepted by all citizens as the sole national language. As an official language, English is used in a variety of public functions: in government, in the law courts, in broadcasting, in the press and in education. In many African and Asian countries, it serves as the means of interpersonal communication between speakers of different indigenous languages. Because of both its national and international reach, English is often used for literature, sometimes in forms that draw heavily on local colloquial forms of English. Writers and politicians in some African and Asian countries are ambivalent about the role of English: English may be viewed as an imperialist language, imposed by colonial oppressors and impeding the role of indigenous languages, or as the language of liberation and nationalism in countries divided by tribal loyalties.
>
> The problem in calculating the numbers of second-language speakers is how to decide who counts as a speaker of the language. Should we include in our totals those who have a rudimentary knowledge of vocabulary and grammar but can make themselves understood only in certain types of exchanges – for example, giving street directions or offering goods for sale? If so, we might recognize as second language speakers perhaps most of the 2.5 billion that have lived in countries where English is used as a second language. On the other hand, conservative estimates, requiring much greater competence in the language, tend to put the number at about 300 million.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Model summary (≤150 words):**
>
> **The Global Spread of English**
>
> English is more widely spread than any other language in history. It is the main first language in some countries, an official or joint official language in many others, and a second language in still others, across all continents, covering about half the world's population. It serves both for communication within these countries and as an international foreign language. Its first-language speakers, over 300 million, live mainly in the USA, Britain, Canada and Australia, where bilingualism is also common. Most second-language countries are former British colonies that kept English after independence because no local language was acceptable to all; there it is used in government, law, the media, education, inter-ethnic communication and literature, although some see it as imperialist while others see it as unifying. The number of second-language speakers is hard to count because it depends on how much competence qualifies someone as a speaker. (about 150 words)
>
> _Outline alternative:_ (1) Unique spread: first, official and second language worldwide. (2) Internal and international uses. (3) First-language speakers: numbers and bilingualism. (4) Second-language countries: former colonies; official functions; mixed attitudes. (5) Difficulty of counting second-language speakers.

Study the passage below carefully and write a **SUMMARY** of it in **not more than 110 words**. Provide your summary with a **heading**.

> The means of transportation has changed and improved over many centuries. Long ago, during the times of the kings and knights, animals such as horses, buffaloes and camels were used by man for transportation purposes. These animals no doubt did save man from traveling by foot; they took a long time to complete the journeys especially when transporting goods.
>
> In 1825, George Stephenson's opening of the first railway marked a significant progress in the history of transportation. Railways were in popular demand because they could carry more people and loads. More importantly, they ran faster than animals. Railways improved the communication networks and hence, imports and exports of goods and people traveling out of their towns or even countries to work were made possible. Unfortunately, since the invention of motor vehicles, the popularity of railways has declined.
>
> Motor vehicles were first invented in the eighteenth century. These vehicles were preferred by many people as they do not run on tracks and hence do not have fixed routes. Travelers can then plan their own routes to suit their convenience. This is especially so when the destinations are places like small towns or remote areas. In these places, few or even none of the trains ever reach them; so traveling by the motor vehicle would solve this problem. Over many years of modifications, the motor vehicle is now one of the most commonly used means of transportation. Today, we travel in cars, taxis, buses, lorries or vans almost every day.
>
> Another form of transportation is by water. It may be the slowest but definitely the cheapest form of bulk transportation. Though over the centuries of innovations, water transportation has improved from the ancient wind dependent yachts to the modern motor driven ships, journeys by water are still characterized by the dangers and unpredictability of meeting natural disasters like the storms.
>
> The evolution of world transportation has reached its pinnacle with the invention of airplanes. Transportation by planes is the easiest and fastest. Planes gliding smoothly in the air are not obstructed by seas, hills, buildings and so on. Though convenient, this means of transport is the most expensive. Despite the popular demand, the transportation network of the planes is still not a balanced and complete one till today. Developed countries tend to make use of air transportation more frequently than the less developed ones as they do more exporting and importing of goods and also have more people traveling to and fro their countries. Hence, the networks in these developed countries are denser.

>
> **The Evolution of Transportation**
>
> Transportation has improved greatly over the centuries. Early people used animals, which spared them walking but were slow, especially for goods. Railways, beginning in 1825, carried more people and goods faster and boosted trade and travel, but declined after motor vehicles appeared. Motor vehicles became the most popular means because, free of tracks, they reach any destination, including remote towns. Water transport is the slowest but cheapest for bulk goods, though storms still make it risky. Air transport, the peak of this development, is the fastest and easiest but the most expensive, and its networks are densest in developed countries. (about 105 words)
>
> _Outline alternative:_ (1) Animals: slow. (2) Railways: faster, more capacity; now declining. (3) Motor vehicles: flexible routes; most common. (4) Water: cheapest, slowest, risky. (5) Air: fastest, costliest; uneven networks.

Read the following passage carefully and write an **outline** or **summary** of it. The summary should be between **100 and 120 words**.

> Philosophy of Education is a label applied to the study of the purpose, process, nature and ideals of education. It can be considered a branch of both philosophy and education. Education can be defined as the teaching and learning of specific skills, and the imparting of knowledge, judgment and wisdom, and is something broader than the societal institution of education we often speak of.
>
> Many educationalists consider it a weak and woolly field, too far removed from the practical applications of the real world to be useful. But philosophers dating back to Plato and the Ancient Greeks have given the area much thought and emphasis, and there is little doubt that their work has helped shape the practice of education over the millennia.
>
> Plato is the earliest important educational thinker, and education is an essential element in "The Republic" (his most important work on philosophy and political theory, written around 360 B.C.). In it, he advocates some rather extreme methods: removing children from their mothers' care and raising them as wards of the state, and differentiating children suitable to the various castes, the highest receiving the most education, so that they could act as guardians of the city and care for the less able. He believed that education should be holistic, including facts, skills, physical discipline, music and art. Plato believed that talent and intelligence is not distributed genetically and thus is to be found in children born to all classes, although his proposed system of selective public education for an educated minority of the population does not really follow a democratic model.
>
> Aristotle considered human nature, habit and reason to be equally important forces to be cultivated in education, the ultimate aim of which should be to produce good and virtuous citizens. He proposed that teachers lead their students systematically, and that repetition be used as a key tool to develop good habits, unlike Socrates' emphasis on questioning his listeners to bring out their own ideas. He emphasized the balancing of the theoretical and practical aspects of subjects taught, among which he explicitly mentions reading, writing, mathematics, music, physical education, literature, history, and a wide range of sciences, as well as play, which he also considered important.
>
> During the Medieval period, the idea of Perennialism was first formulated by St. Thomas Aquinas in his work "De Magistro". Perennialism holds that one should teach those things deemed to be of everlasting importance to all people everywhere, namely principles and reasoning, not just facts (which are apt to change over time), and that one should teach first about people, not machines or techniques. It was originally religious in nature, and it was only much later that a theory of secular perennialism developed.
>
> During the Renaissance, the French skeptic Michel de Montaigne (1533 – 1592) was one of the first to critically look at education. Unusually for his time, Montaigne was willing to question the conventional wisdom of the period, calling into question the whole edifice of the educational system, and the implicit assumption that university-educated philosophers were necessarily wiser than uneducated farm workers, for example.

> **Model summary (100–120 words):**
>
> **Philosophy of Education and Its Early Thinkers**
>
> Philosophy of education studies the purpose, process, nature and ideals of education, which is broader than schooling. Though some think it impractical, it has shaped educational practice since ancient Greece. Plato wanted the state to raise children and educate them according to class, with the most able trained as guardians, and favoured a holistic curriculum, believing talent exists in every class. Aristotle aimed to produce virtuous citizens by cultivating nature, habit and reason through systematic teaching and repetition, balancing theory and practice across many subjects, including play. In the Middle Ages, Aquinas's perennialism stressed lasting principles and reasoning, and in the Renaissance Montaigne questioned the educational system and the supposed superiority of the educated. (about 118 words)
>
> _Outline alternative:_ (1) Definition and scope. (2) Value despite criticism. (3) Plato: state-raised children; class-based, holistic education. (4) Aristotle: virtue through habit and reason; balanced curriculum. (5) Aquinas: perennialism. (6) Montaigne: critical questioning of education.
